blocks.heading: The first ezer: Adam's search for a partner

paragraphs.text: The Rav opens with the Midrash about the first samech in the Torah, at the creation of the woman. Since the Torah is the blueprint of the world, the first 'ezer' (helper) it mentions defines what help is, and that ezer is the woman.
Adam went around to all the animals looking for a partner and found none. Only when Hashem cast sleep on him and took his rib did he open his eyes and recognize his ezer.

From this the Rav learns that a person cannot get his ezer by running around; it comes from Hashem, as the passuk in Tehillim 121 says. He brings the Midrash on the kings: Chizkiyahu said he would sleep and Hashem would fight his war, and in the middle of the Pesach night Sancheriv's camp was destroyed.

Yaakov is the father of bitachon. According to the Midrash he fled with nothing, while Eliezer had come with ten camels, yet he did not lose his trust. The sukkah, a flimsy hut that the rain and wind enter, is the shelter of bitachon, and the Mishnah on sukkah speaks of sleeping, because only one who feels secure can sleep.

blocks.heading: Levels of bitachon and the lesson of bitul

paragraphs.text: The Rav cites the Chovos Halevavos in Shaar HaBitachon against thinking one must chase a second and third job. With the manna, as the Gemara in Yoma describes, some ran out early and others went farther, while the tzaddikim who davened and learned found it at their door. The first ezer came after all of Adam's efforts failed: a lesson in bitul.

blocks.heading: Rashi's question and the three Torahs

paragraphs.text: The Rav brings Rashi's question on the first passuk: why does the Torah not begin with the first mitzvah given to Yisrael? Rashi answers with the passuk in Tehillim 111: if the nations call the Jews robbers, they can reply that Hashem created the world and gave the land to whom He wished. The Rav asks why the nations still cry 'robbers' today.
He explains that the Torah contains three Torahs: of creation, of man, which belongs to the nations as well, and of Yisrael. The Torah of creation begins with the first passuk of Bereishis.

blocks.heading: Nature is a Torah, and a miracle changes it

paragraphs.text: The Gemara in Shabbos 53b tells of a poor man who could not hire a nursemaid, and a miracle let him nurse his infant himself. Yet the Gemara remarks how lowly he was that the order of creation was changed for him.

To explain this, the Rav says that all of nature is written in the pesukim of Bereishis. Whole masechtos rest on a few words, as Gittin rests on the passuk in Devarim 24:1, and the Tannaim and Amoraim had a whole Gemara on Bereishis, of which very little has reached us.

So a bird that flies fulfills the passuk in Bereishis 1:20, like a Jew putting on tefillin, and a tree that gives fruit fulfills Bereishis 1:11; the only difference is that man has free choice. A miracle therefore changes the Torah, and tzaddikim held back from making miracles.

Next comes the Torah of man: Hashem put all of nature under man, as Dovid HaMelech says in Tehillim 8:7, and the Gemara in Sanhedrin 56b derives the seven mitzvos of Noach from the passuk in Bereishis 2:16.

If man keeps the Torah of man, creation keeps the Torah of creation, and if not, not. In the generation of the flood even the animals stopped keeping theirs. In the generation of the desert, which learned Torah from Moshe Rabbeinu for forty years, nature flourished so that one cluster of grapes needed eight men; after the churban it declined. Because mankind sinned, Hashem took the control away from them and gave it to Avraham Avinu.

blocks.heading: Three strikes and a last chance

paragraphs.text: The Rav reads Bereishis as three strikes: Adam's sin, the flood and the dispersion, after which the keys of creation passed to Avraham and his children. At the giving of the Torah the nations got a last chance: Hashem went to Esav and to Yishmael, and they refused. All these stories lead up to 'Hachodesh hazeh lachem' in Shemos 12:2.

blocks.heading: Why the nations claim Eretz Yisrael

paragraphs.text: The Rav asks how the nations can claim the land at all. Every land in history was taken by conquest, as America was taken from the Indians, and conquest is a kinyan; the Rambam explains that this is why the kedushah of the land lapsed.

He answers that Eretz Yisrael is different. It is the center of creation, the place from which the world was founded, as in Yoma 54b, and the word Bereishis already hints at the Beis Hamikdash. Therefore everyone feels he must have a share in it: Hevel was killed over it, the Crusades were fought over it, and so tiny a country is on the front page every day.

blocks.heading: All of Bereishis as an introduction

paragraphs.text: Since the Gemara says the most important comes first, the Rav asks why the Torah did not open with Hachodesh, Shemos 12:2. Bereishis is a chapter of history, which the passuk in Devarim 32:8 describes: the nations had their chances and failed, so Hashem chose Avraham and swore the land to the Avos, as in Tehillim 105:9-11. All of it explains why the Torah of Yisrael was given only to the Jews; the nations do not admit it now, but when Mashiach comes they will see the reason.
